t.1.209.2: Made proud by our beauty, by our youth, and by Kandarpa, we did what was improper; you ought to forgive us, O twice-born one.
t.1.209.1: Then all of us, deeply distressed, O best of the Bharatas, went for refuge to that unwavering Brahmin, rich in austerities.
t.1.209.4: Those who reflect on dharma hold that women were created not to be slain. Therefore, in accordance with dharma, O knower of dharma, you should not harm us.
t.1.209.3: This alone is ruin enough for us, O you whose wealth is austerity, that we came here to tempt you, whose self is firmly disciplined.
t.1.209.5: O knower of dharma, a brāhmaṇa is said to be a friend to all beings. May this auspicious saying of the wise prove true.
t.1.209.6: The virtuous give protection to those who have come to them for refuge. We have come to you for refuge; therefore you ought to forgive us.
t.1.209.7: Thus addressed, O hero, the righteous-souled brahmin, a doer of auspicious deeds whose splendour equalled that of the sun and the moon, showed us his grace.
t.1.209.10: Then all of you will regain your own form once more. Never before have I spoken an untruth, not even in jest.
t.1.209.8: “A hundred,” “a thousand,” and “all”: every one of these can express the imperishable. But this “hundred” is a fixed measure; it does not express the imperishable.
t.1.209.11: From this time forth, all those bathing places will become renowned everywhere in this world by the name of Nārītīrthas, the Fords of the Women, and they will be holy and purifying for the wise.
t.1.209.9: And when some best of men drags you out of the water onto dry land, you who have become crocodiles seizing men in the water…
t.1.209.13: Where, then, might all of us, in a short time, come upon that man who would restore us once again to that former form of ours?
t.1.209.12: Then, having saluted that brahmin and walked around him reverently, we went away from that place, deeply distressed, and pondered.
t.1.209.14: Thus we brooded, O Bhārata, and after what seemed but a moment we beheld the greatly fortunate divine seer Nārada.
t.1.209.16: He asked us the root of our sorrow, and we told it to him; and having heard it just as it had happened, he spoke these words.
t.1.209.15: All of us were delighted on seeing him, the divine seer of boundless splendour, and having saluted him, O Pārtha, we stood there with troubled faces.
t.1.209.17: On the southern seacoast there are indeed five sacred fords; go without delay to those holy and delightful places.
t.1.209.18: There the tiger among men, the pure-souled Pāṇḍava Dhanaṃjaya, will swiftly free you from this suffering; of that there is no doubt.
t.1.209.19: Having heard his words, O hero, all of us came here; and today it has indeed come true, for I have been set free by you, O sinless one.
t.1.209.21: Then, O lord of the people, the best of the Pāṇḍavas, mighty and undaunted in spirit, freed every one of them from that curse.
t.1.209.20: But these four others, my friends, are still held in the water. Do this auspicious deed as a hero, and set them all free.
t.1.209.22: Rising from that water and regaining their own bodies, those Apsarases, O king, then appeared as they had been before.
t.1.209.23: Having purified the sacred fords and likewise taken leave of them, the lord went to the city of Maṇalūra to see Citrāṅgadā again.
t.1.209.24: On her he begot a son, King Babhruvāhana. Having seen him, O king, the Pāṇḍava went on toward Gokarṇa.
